text:
Every model in a dbt project now has one more reader: a language model, behind an ask-your-data assistant. It reads the same tables and definitions an analyst does, but it takes them literally, and it answers thousands of questions nobody reviews. Six questions on making that safe, and on knowing when it isn't. Five are worked through, and one quick one comes last.

Question one. Why does text-to-sequel over raw tables give confident wrong answers? Because the hard part of a business question isn't the sequel. It's the definitions the sequel has to encode. Ask for revenue, and an assistant writing sequel against raw tables has to guess. Net of refunds? Cancelled orders? Test accounts? Which of three similar tables, which join path, and does it fan out? Here are eight orders from five customers, and one customer is a test account. Sum every order: fourteen hundred fifty dollars. Only the completed ones: eleven hundred ninety. Completed, and not from the test account: four hundred forty. Each guess is a valid query with a plausible number, and the biggest is more than three times the smallest. Nothing in the sequel would look wrong to the person who asked. That's the failure to name: not an error, but a fluent, plausible, wrong number. And no query can find the right one in the rows. Which reading counts as revenue is a company decision, so it has to be written down where the assistant reads it.
